questions.q: Which order of SN2 nucleophilicity is correct?
options: All three are equal because the attacking atom is oxygen in each
questions.explain: Branching blocks backside attack on carbon, so nucleophilicity falls with bulk even though basicity rises in the order CH₃O⁻ < (CH₃)₂CHO⁻ < (CH₃)₃CO⁻.

questions.q: Arrange CH₃COO⁻, CH₃O⁻ and C₆H₅O⁻ in decreasing nucleophilicity.
questions.explain: With the same attacking atom (O), nucleophilicity follows basicity; resonance spreads the charge in phenoxide and even more in acetate, weakening both.

questions.q: In a protic solvent, CH₃S⁻ is a better nucleophile than CH₃O⁻ although it is a weaker base. This is an example of:
options: Nucleophilicity following basicity for the same attacking atom
Nucleophilicity rising down a group in protic solvents, because the larger anion is less strongly hydrogen-bonded
questions.explain: Down a group in protic solvents the large, polarisable anion is caged less by hydrogen bonds and attacks faster, so nucleophilicity and basicity run in opposite directions.

questions.q: A secondary alkyl bromide is heated with potassium tert-butoxide. The main pathway and reason are:
options: SN2, because tert-butoxide is a strong nucleophile
SN1, because tert-butoxide is a weak base
Williamson ether synthesis, because alkoxides always substitute
E2, because tert-butoxide is a strong base but a hindered, poor nucleophile
questions.explain: Its bulk blocks backside attack on carbon but a surface β-hydrogen is still easy to reach, so it removes protons and drives E2 instead of SN2.
